introduction: The readings of this guide speak of sacrifice as the condition of every higher life: the seed that gives itself to become a tree, the self that is forgotten in service, the lover who gives all for the Beloved. They distinguish the outward sacrifice of life from the inward one of living in obedience and for others, honour the martyrs, recall the sufferings of the Báb and Bahá’u’lláh as borne for the world, and end in prayers that offer everything. The idea is among the oldest in religion, and the quotations beside the readings trace it through Abraham and his son in Genesis and the Qur’an, the grain of wheat and the cross, Paul’s living sacrifice, the Gita’s offering of every act, and Confucius and Mencius on giving up life for what is right. Those that stand against the readings matter here: the prophets who wanted mercy and not sacrifice, Paul’s warning that a body given to be burned may profit nothing, Wilfred Owen on the old lie, and Nietzsche’s remark that blood proves no truth.
questions: The readings say that to live in obedience and service can be harder than to die for a cause. What does a day of that kind of sacrifice look like?
The grain of wheat dies and bears fruit; Rumi says he was never made less by dying. What have you given up that turned out to be a gain?
Hosea and Micah wanted mercy and justice, not offerings, and Paul says a sacrifice without love profits nothing. What do the readings say makes a sacrifice acceptable?
Nietzsche held that blood is the worst witness to truth, and Owen called dying for one’s country the old lie. How do you tell a true sacrifice from a wasted or a mistaken one?
Adam Smith thought daily life runs on self-interest. Where, in a family or a community you know, does it visibly run on something else?
The last readings are prayers that offer everything. Which words in them could you honestly say, and which would you have to grow into?

outside.why: Jesus tells his disciples that whoever would be great among them must serve, as he came to give his life.
The Gospel states the paradox on which this reading rests: whoever will lose his life shall find it.
Emerson's counsel runs the other way: trust thyself, for every heart vibrates to that iron string. Is forgetting the self the opposite of trusting it, or might they meet?
Paul could say that for him to live is Christ and to die is gain: either way his life was no longer his own.
Jesus gives the image that the readings return to: unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone.
Paul describes this dying to self from the inside: I am crucified with Christ; nevertheless I live, yet not I.
John's Gospel measures love by this: that a man lay down his life for his friends.
Isaiah speaks of one who was wounded for others' transgressions, and by whose stripes they are healed.
Paul asks for a living sacrifice, which he calls a reasonable service: the body presented, the mind renewed.
Paul says he counts everything he had gained as loss for the sake of what he has come to know.
Luke's Gospel adds one word to the saying about the cross: daily.
Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to the arena, called himself God's wheat, to be ground by the teeth of beasts.
Paul says that though he give his body to be burned and have not love, it profits him nothing. What is it in a sacrifice that counts, if the outward act is not it?
The psalm says that the sacrifice God wants is a broken spirit and a contrite heart.
The first letter of John draws the conclusion for ordinary life: whoever sees a brother in need and shuts his heart has not this love.

Adam Smith observed that we expect our dinner from the butcher and the baker out of regard to their own interest, not their benevolence. Can a community live by the rule of this reading and not by his?
Tertullian reports what the neighbours said of the early Christians: see how they love one another, and are ready to die for one another.
The commandment to honour father and mother stands among the ten, with a promise attached.
Jesus watched a poor widow put in two small coins and said she had given more than all, because she gave her whole living.
George Eliot ends her novel by saying that the growing good of the world depends partly on unhistoric acts and hidden lives.
Peter says to Jesus, we have left all and followed thee, and is told what such leaving receives.
Job's first word after losing everything was that the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.
The Qur’an says that no one attains piety until he spends of what he loves.
The Preacher advises against being righteous over much: why shouldest thou destroy thyself? What would he make of a wish for a thousand mansions to lose?
The Qur’an speaks of a bargain in which God has bought from the believers their lives and their wealth.
Krishna asks that whatever one does, eats, gives or endures be done as an offering.
Jesus told a rich young man to sell what he had and follow, and the young man went away sorrowful.
Luke records the saying in its hardest form: whoever does not forsake all that he has cannot be my disciple.
Paul and Barnabas told the new churches that the kingdom is entered through much tribulation.
The Letter to the Hebrews reads hardship as a mark of love: whom the Lord loves He chastens.
The Gita says that for one whose heart is set on truth every work is a work of sacrifice.
Jesus sets the two kinds of striving side by side: saving one's life and losing it.

Wilfred Owen, who died in the trenches, called it the old lie that it is sweet and fitting to die for one's country. How should the sacrifices of soldiers be spoken of beside the sacrifice these readings ask?
The first letter to Timothy says that we brought nothing into this world and can carry nothing out.
The Qur’an says that those who believe are stauncher in their love for God than others are for what they worship.
Paul tells the Corinthians that he will very gladly spend and be spent for them.
Mencius says that he likes life and likes righteousness, and that if he cannot keep both he will let life go.
Confucius says that the person of virtue will not seek to live at the cost of virtue, and will even give up life to keep it whole.
Paul speaks of things prepared that no eye has seen and that have not entered the human heart.
Paul reckons that the sufferings of the present time are not worthy to be compared with what shall be revealed.
Paul blesses the God of all comfort, who comforts people in tribulation so that they can comfort others.
The psalm has the same picture of scattering and harvest: they that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Hillel asked the question that every generation has to answer for itself: and if not now, when?
Paul's hymn follows the same curve: he made himself of no reputation and humbled himself, wherefore God highly exalted him.
The church at Smyrna is told: be faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life.
Nietzsche said that blood is the very worst witness to truth, since people have died for every kind of cause. What, beyond the willingness to die, makes a sacrifice a testimony?
Ruth's promise to Naomi is faithfulness in its plainest words: whither thou goest, I will go.
The letter to the Ephesians asks its readers to walk in love as Christ did, who gave himself as an offering.
Paul, at the end, writes that he is now ready to be offered and that the time of his departure is at hand.
The apostles left the council rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for the name.
Paul speaks of one who took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death.
Jesus says of himself that the good shepherd gives his life for the sheep.
Socrates told his judges that a man who is good for anything does not calculate the chance of living or dying, only whether he is doing right.
Paul answered friends who begged him not to go that he was ready not only to be bound but to die.
The Qur’an gives the believer these words: my worship and my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for God.
The Qur’an speaks of the one who would sell his very self, seeking the pleasure of God.
Paul remarks how rare it is that anyone will die even for a good man.
Job reaches the limit of trust: though He slay me, yet will I trust in Him.
This is the command the Báb's prayer recalls: take now thy son, thine only son, whom thou lovest.
Hosea heard God say: I desired mercy and not sacrifice. How do the prophets' warnings about sacrifice bear on a prayer to offer a thousand sons?
The old bishop Polycarp, facing the fire, said that he had served his King eighty-six years and would not deny Him now.
In Genesis the knife is stayed and the son returns alive from the altar. What does it mean that in this reading the sacrifice does not return?
Stephen died under the stones calling on his Lord and asking that the sin not be laid to his killers' charge.
The Letter to the Hebrews says of those who were mocked, scourged and slain that the world was not worthy of them.
The Qur’an says of those slain in God's way: think not of them as dead; they are living.
The psalm says that precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints.
Ignatius of Loyola's prayer makes the same offering in life: take, Lord, my liberty, my memory, my understanding, my whole will.
In Revelation those in white robes are they who came out of great tribulation.
Jesus says that whoever loves father or mother more than him is not worthy of him.
Dickens gives his hero, going to the scaffold in another's place, the words: it is a far, far better thing that I do.
The Qur’an says: call not those who are slain in the way of God dead; they are living, though you perceive it not.
Bunyan's Valiant-for-truth crosses the river, and all the trumpets sound for him on the other side.
The Letter to the Hebrews says of the faithful that they confessed they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth.
Lincoln wrote to a mother of the solemn pride that must be hers to have laid so costly a sacrifice upon the altar of freedom.
At Gettysburg Lincoln said that it is for the living to be dedicated to the unfinished work of those who fought there.
David refused a gift of land for his altar: he would not offer to the Lord what cost him nothing.
Micah asks whether he should give his firstborn for his transgression, and the prophet's answer turns to justice, mercy and humility. What is the most precious thing a person can offer?
The psalmist trusts that his wanderings are counted and his tears kept in God's book.
At his arrest Jesus says: the cup which my Father has given me, shall I not drink it?
The first letter of Peter tells its readers to rejoice in the fiery trial, as sharers in Christ's sufferings.
The Song of Songs says that love is strong as death and that many waters cannot quench it.
In the parable the merchant sells all that he has for one pearl.
Rumi's reed sings of the pain of separation, and says that whoever has been parted from his source longs to return.
The buyer in the parable sells everything for joy, to have the field where the treasure is hid.
The Imitation of Christ says that love makes every heavy thing light and bears every hardship as nothing.
Rumi says: I died as mineral and became a plant, died as plant and rose to animal; when was I ever made less by dying?
In the Qur’an it is the son who says: O my father, do that which thou art commanded; thou shalt find me steadfast.
Jephthah's rash vow cost him his daughter, and the book records his grief without praising him. When is readiness to give everything a virtue, and when is it a vow that should never have been made?
Paul explains his own life in the same way: the love of Christ constrains us.
In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup might pass, and then: nevertheless not as I will, but as Thou wilt.
The psalmist's soul longs as a deer pants for the water brooks.
Ezekiel is told to call the breath from the four winds to breathe on the slain, that they may live.
Rabi‘a asked to be denied Paradise if she worshipped in hope of it. Is the crown in this prayer a reward for the sacrifice, or the sacrifice itself?
The Letter to the Hebrews speaks of a sacrifice of praise, and of doing good and sharing as sacrifices that please God.
The sages taught: be like servants who serve the master without expecting a reward.
Paul says he glories in tribulations, because of what they work in a person.
Isaiah hears God say: fear thou not, for I am with thee; be not dismayed.
The Qur’an says of offerings that their flesh does not reach God; what reaches Him is the devotion of the one who offers.
The psalmist would sooner be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of the great.
David's prayer at the offering for the temple begins by confessing that everything in heaven and earth is already God's.

hebrews-sacrifice-of-praise.text: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased

john-epistle-lay-down-our-lives.text: Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us: and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren. But whoso hath this world's good, and seeth his brother have need, and shutteth up his bowels of compassion from him, how dwelleth the love of God in him

mark-we-have-left-all.text: Then Peter began to say unto him, Lo, we have left all, and have followed thee. And Jesus answered and said, Verily I say unto you, There is no man that hath left house, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my sake, and the gospel's, But he shall receive an hundredfold now in this time, houses, and brethren, and sisters, and mothers, and children, and lands, with persecutions; and in the world to come eternal life

luke-take-up-his-cross-daily.text: And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me

samuel-cost-me-nothing.text: And the king said unto Araunah, Nay; but I will surely buy it of thee at a price: neither will I offer burnt offerings unto the Lord my God of that which doth cost me nothing

corinthians-spend-and-be-spent.text: And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved

matthew-not-as-i-will.text: And he went a little farther, and fell on his face, and prayed, saying, O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt

corinthians-body-to-be-burned.text: And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing

ephesians-offering-and-a-sacrifice.text: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children; And walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour

genesis-take-now-thy-son.text: And he said, Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering upon one of the mountains which I will tell thee of

romans-for-a-good-man.text: For scarcely for a righteous man will one die: yet peradventure for a good man some would even dare to die. But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us

judges-jephthah.text: And it came to pass, when he saw her, that he rent his clothes, and said, Alas, my daughter! thou hast brought me very low, and thou art one of them that trouble me: for I have opened my mouth unto the Lord, and I cannot go back

quran-do-that-which-thou-art-commanded.text: And when (his son) was old enough to walk with him, (Abraham) said: O my dear son, I have seen in a dream that I must sacrifice thee. So look, what thinkest thou? He said: O my father! Do that which thou art commanded. Allah willing, thou shalt find me of the steadfast. Then, when they had both surrendered (to Allah), and he had flung him down upon his face, We called unto him: O Abraham! Thou hast already fulfilled the vision. Lo! thus do We reward the good. Lo! that verily was a clear test. Then We ransomed him with a tremendous victim

quran-sell-himself.text: And of mankind is he who would sell himself, seeking the pleasure of Allah; and Allah hath compassion on (His) bondmen.

quran-flesh-and-blood-reach-not.text: Their flesh and their food reach not Allah, but the devotion from you reacheth Him. Thus have We made them subject unto you that ye may magnify Allah that He hath guided you. And give good tidings (O Muhammad) to the good.

analects-sacrifice-their-lives.text: The determined scholar and the man of virtue will not seek to live at the expense of injuring their virtue. They will even sacrifice their lives to preserve their virtue complete
analects-sacrifice-their-lives.author: Confucius

plato-not-to-calculate.text: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong - acting the part of a good man or of a bad
plato-not-to-calculate.author: Plato

mencius-life-and-righteousness.text: So, I like life, and I also like righteousness. If I cannot keep the two together, I will let life go, and choose righteousness
mencius-life-and-righteousness.author: Mencius

gita-sacrifice-is-brahm.text: of such an one What work he does is work of sacrifice, Which passeth purely into ash and smoke Consumed upon the altar! All's then God! The sacrifice is Brahm, the ghee and grain Are Brahm, the fire is Brahm
